Can a power station run a diesel heater, and for how long?

Scenarios Updated 2026-08-08

Yes, on nearly any power station in this library — a diesel air heater is one of the smallest electrical loads we cover, because the heat comes from burning fuel rather than from the battery. The electronics only fire the glow plug and turn the combustion fan.

The one figure worth checking is the start: Eberspächer states the glow plug pulls up to 100 W and holds it for a minute or two while it ignites, and that duration puts it outside what a surge rating describes. So it is not a spike and is not added to any start-up total — it is checked against continuous output for the whole of that time, which is the harder of the two tests, and even a small station clears it.

Where the heat actually comes from

From Eberspächer’s own technical description, corroborated by Webasto’s spec page for a comparable unit. Heat output for this class runs into the low thousands of watts; none of it is electrical.

Not a separate state from the row above — the same low fan-only draw.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · diesel heater record

A heater rated at over two kilowatts of warmth drawing 34 W of electricity is not a typo. The fuel supplies the heat; the 12 V or 24 V electrical side only fires the igniter, runs the fuel pump and spins the combustion and cabin fans. That is why this is the one heating appliance in our library that a small power station handles without strain.

A start-up that lasts minutes, not milliseconds

The glow-plug start

Eberspächer states this explicitly rather than us deriving it: the glow plug stays powered for roughly a minute after ignition is detected, which changes how it has to be checked.

At start-up 100 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

The glow plug, firing the igniter. Modest in watts; unusual in duration.

How long it lasts 60,000 ms Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

Roughly a minute — far outside the fraction-of-a-second window a motor’s inrush occupies.

Start-up ratio 2.9 × Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

A modest multiple at the top setting and a much larger one at the lowest — the ratio depends entirely on which running figure it is measured against, which is exactly why our engine does not size this appliance off a ratio at all.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · diesel heater record · manufacturer technical description

A minute-long load is not a surge in any sense a power station’s spec sheet uses the word. Every other inrush in our library is measured in milliseconds; this one is measured in minutes, which means an inverter cannot simply absorb it and move on — it has to sustain that draw the way it sustains any other continuous load. Our engine treats a start-up this long as continuous rather than as a momentary spike, checked against the machine’s continuous output rather than its surge ceiling.

Even the smallest machine in the library clears it

One heater, two machines

Live engine runs — and the start-up figure on each reading line needs reading carefully. This site reports no separate surge demand for this load, because there is no spike to report, so the watts printed beside "at start-up" are the running draw. The glow plug’s 100 W is held rather than spiked, so it is left out of any start-up total and checked against continuous output instead, for the whole of that time. Both tests clear here with room to spare.

BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 × diesel air heater 34 W running · 100 W held at start-up, checked against continuous output 5.7%
5.7 h

The check that matters on this row: the glow plug’s 100 W, held for 60 seconds or more, against 600 W of continuous output — not against a surge rating, which describes an event lasting a second or two and does not apply here. The smallest runtime-capable machine in our library, and still an easy clear.

Dial it down and the number changes a great deal

That figure is the top control setting, which most nights do not need. At the lowest setting the heater draws a small fraction of the top figure, and the same battery stretches to several times the runtime above — the thermostat on most of these units already steps down automatically once the space is warm.

The wiring is usually the real decision

A permanent installation typically runs straight off a vehicle’s 12 V or 24 V house battery rather than through a portable power station at all — the load is small enough that the two are electrically interchangeable, and the real choice is whether you already have a house battery or need something you can move between a tent, a van and a garage.

Questions people ask

What size power station do I need for a diesel heater?
Smaller than the heat output suggests. The heater burns fuel for warmth and only draws electricity to fire the glow plug and run the fans, so even a compact power station covers the running load and the roughly 100 W, minute-long start with room to spare.
How long will a power station run a diesel heater?
Long enough for a full night on most portable batteries at the top setting, and considerably longer at a lower one — the heater draws only a few dozen watts even at its most demanding control setting, a small fraction of what most power stations hold.
Why does the start-up figure matter if it is only 100 W?
Because of how long it lasts, not how big it is. The glow plug stays powered for roughly a minute while it ignites — long enough that it has to be treated as a continuous draw rather than a momentary surge, a different check than the one a sump pump or a compressor triggers.
